questions.question_text: For the data set {4, 8, 8, 10, 20}, the median is:
questions.explanation: Ordered, the middle (3rd of 5) value is 8. The median is the center value; with 5 values it's the third one.

questions.question_text: A value with a z-score of +2.0 lies:
questions.option_b: 2 standard deviations above the mean
questions.explanation: A z-score measures distance from the mean in standard deviations; +2.0 means two SDs above the mean. z-scores standardize values for comparison.

questions.question_text: The interquartile range (IQR) equals:
questions.option_b: Q3 minus Q1
questions.explanation: IQR = Q3 − Q1, the spread of the middle 50% of data. It's resistant to outliers and used in the 1.5×IQR outlier rule.

questions.question_text: The coefficient of determination r² represents the:
questions.option_b: proportion of variation in y explained by the linear model
questions.explanation: r² (between 0 and 1) is the fraction of the response's variability explained by the regression on x. An r² of 0.81 means 81% is explained.

questions.question_text: If r = 0.6, then r² equals:
questions.explanation: r² = 0.6² = 0.36, so 36% of the variation in y is explained by the linear model. Squaring the correlation gives the coefficient of determination.

questions.question_text: Blinding in an experiment is used to reduce:
questions.option_b: bias from expectations (placebo and experimenter effects)
questions.explanation: Blinding keeps subjects (and ideally evaluators) unaware of treatment assignment, controlling for expectation-driven bias. Double-blinding blinds both parties.

questions.question_text: A confounding variable is one that:
questions.option_b: is associated with both the explanatory and response variables, muddying the relationship
questions.explanation: A confounder is linked to both variables, making it impossible to attribute effects to the explanatory variable alone. Randomization in experiments controls confounders.

questions.question_text: If P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.3 and they are mutually exclusive, P(A or B) =
questions.explanation: For mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) = 0.4 + 0.3 = 0.7 (no overlap to subtract). They can't occur together.

questions.question_text: The expected value of rolling a fair six-sided die is:
questions.explanation: E(X) = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5. The expected value is the probability-weighted average of outcomes.

questions.question_text: The mean of the sampling distribution of the sample mean equals:
questions.option_b: the population mean μ
questions.explanation: The sampling distribution of x̄ is centered at the population mean μ (x̄ is an unbiased estimator). Its spread shrinks as sample size grows.

questions.question_text: Bias in an estimator refers to:
questions.option_b: a systematic tendency to over- or under-estimate the true parameter
questions.explanation: Bias is a consistent directional error—the sampling distribution centers away from the true value. Variability is the spread; the two are distinct qualities.

questions.question_text: To cut the margin of error in half (same confidence), you must:
questions.option_b: quadruple the sample size
questions.explanation: Margin of error ∝ 1/√n, so halving it requires multiplying n by 4. Precision improves with the square root of sample size.

questions.question_text: A P-value of 0.02 means:
questions.option_a: the null hypothesis is true with probability 0.02
questions.option_b: if the null were true, results this extreme would occur about 2% of the time
questions.explanation: The P-value is the probability of data as or more extreme than observed, assuming H₀ is true. It is NOT the probability that H₀ is true—a common misinterpretation.

questions.question_text: Degrees of freedom for a one-sample t-test with n = 25 is:
questions.explanation: For a one-sample t-test, df = n − 1 = 24. Degrees of freedom adjust the t-distribution's shape for sample size.

questions.question_text: Failing to reject H₀ means:
questions.option_b: there is insufficient evidence against H₀, not proof it is true
questions.explanation: Failing to reject H₀ means the evidence wasn't strong enough to reject it—not that it's true. Statistics never 'accepts' or proves the null.

questions.question_text: Degrees of freedom for a chi-square goodness-of-fit test with 5 categories is:
questions.explanation: For goodness-of-fit, df = number of categories − 1 = 5 − 1 = 4. Tests of independence use (rows−1)(columns−1) instead.

questions.question_text: In a regression equation ŷ = 3 + 2x, predicting y when x = 5 gives:
questions.explanation: ŷ = 3 + 2(5) = 3 + 10 = 13. Substitute the x-value into the least-squares equation to predict y.

questions.question_text: A value is flagged as an outlier by the 1.5×IQR rule if it falls below:
questions.option_b: Q1 − 1.5×IQR (or above Q3 + 1.5×IQR)
questions.explanation: The 1.5×IQR rule flags values below Q1 − 1.5×IQR or above Q3 + 1.5×IQR as outliers. It's the standard boxplot outlier criterion.

questions.question_text: Extrapolation in regression means:
questions.option_b: predicting outside the range of the observed x-values, which is risky
questions.explanation: Extrapolation predicts beyond the observed data range, where the linear pattern may not hold—an unreliable practice. Interpolation (within range) is safer.

questions.question_text: Voluntary response samples are biased because:
questions.option_b: people with strong opinions are more likely to respond
questions.explanation: Self-selected (voluntary response) samples over-represent those with strong feelings, skewing results. Random sampling avoids this bias.

questions.question_text: The complement of an event A, written Aᶜ, has probability:
questions.explanation: The complement (A not occurring) has probability 1 − P(A), since all outcomes sum to 1. The complement rule simplifies many calculations.

questions.question_text: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̄ is:
questions.option_b: σ/√n
questions.explanation: The standard error of the mean is σ/√n, which decreases as n increases—larger samples give more precise estimates of μ.

questions.question_text: Increasing the sample size in a confidence interval (same confidence level) makes the interval:
questions.option_b: narrower (more precise)
questions.explanation: A larger sample reduces the standard error, narrowing the interval and improving precision. Bigger samples give tighter estimates.

questions.question_text: A matched-pairs t-test is appropriate when data are:
questions.option_b: paired (e.g., before-and-after measurements on the same subjects)
questions.explanation: Matched-pairs designs analyze the differences within pairs (before/after, twins), using a one-sample t-test on the differences. It controls for individual variation.

questions.question_text: A chi-square goodness-of-fit test compares observed counts to:
questions.option_b: expected counts based on a hypothesized distribution
questions.explanation: Goodness-of-fit checks whether observed category counts match a claimed distribution (expected counts). Large discrepancies yield a large χ² and small P-value.

questions.question_text: The y-intercept of a regression line is the predicted y when x equals:
questions.explanation: The intercept is ŷ when x = 0. It may lack practical meaning if x = 0 is outside the data range or unrealistic.

questions.question_text: Adding a constant of 10 to every value in a dataset changes the standard deviation by:
questions.option_b: nothing (it stays the same)
questions.explanation: Adding a constant shifts all values equally, leaving the spread (SD) unchanged. Only multiplying values scales the SD.

questions.question_text: A binomial setting requires a fixed number of trials, independent trials, two outcomes, and:
questions.option_b: a constant probability of success
questions.explanation: The binomial conditions (BINS): Binary outcomes, Independent trials, fixed Number of trials, and Same probability each trial. All four must hold.

questions.question_text: Lowering the significance level α from 0.05 to 0.01 makes it:
questions.option_b: harder to reject H₀ (requires stronger evidence)
questions.explanation: A smaller α demands a smaller P-value to reject H₀, reducing Type I error risk but raising Type II error risk. It sets a stricter evidence bar.
